claims.text: Molecular dynamics simulations, potentially augmented by Monte Carlo exchange methods, can be used to study the thermal response of FeCuCrCoNi nanoparticles.
Atomistic simulations can reveal diameter-dependent changes in surface segregation and atomic ordering during heating.
The initial FeCuCrCoNi nanoparticles are synthesized, equiatomic, and largely chemically disordered.
The proposed simulations compare gradually heated nanoparticles with diameters spanning approximately 2–10 nm.
NVT simulations using validated multicomponent interatomic potentials and a sufficiently long heating schedule can capture diffusion and ordering events in FeCuCrCoNi nanoparticles.
Surface segregation and short-range order evolve with nanoparticle size during heating.
The higher surface-to-volume ratio of smaller nanoparticles enhances thermally activated atomic diffusion and surface segregation.
Surface segregation can drive progressive phase separation during heating of high-entropy nanoalloys.
Smaller FeCuCrCoNi nanoparticles undergo structural rearrangement or phase separation at lower temperatures than larger particles.
Larger FeCuCrCoNi nanoparticles possess more bulk-like stability that delays thermally induced structural changes.
Smaller FeCuCrCoNi nanoparticles will show substantial ordering changes, coalescence, or phase transformation at lower temperatures.
Larger FeCuCrCoNi nanoparticles will retain a disordered structure over a wider temperature range.
The onset temperature for thermal destabilization increases with FeCuCrCoNi nanoparticle size.
Prior MD and MD–MC studies of other high-entropy alloys demonstrate temperature- or configuration-dependent short-range ordering and atomic displacement behavior.
The cited prior studies provide a baseline without strong nanoparticle-size dependence.
Simulation time scales, interatomic-potential accuracy, and the investigated size range limit the applicability of the predictions.
Quantitative transformation-onset temperatures remain uncertain and require calibration against experiments such as in situ heating TEM.
A lack of size dependence in the onset of structural reorganization, or failure of smaller particles to be less thermally stable under identical conditions, would falsify the hypothesis.

contradictions.description: Coalescence is predicted, but the stated design only specifies nanoparticles of different diameters and an NVT heating protocol; it does not specify simulations containing multiple particles in contact or close enough to coalesce.
